# CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU

Deng Pan^(\*), Xue-Jian Gao, Junyi Fan, Bin Du, Jiasheng Li,
Xinxian Chen, Nok Yan Chang, Xinlin Li, Lingchao Zheng, Jun Li,
Yuwei Fan Huawei

###### Abstract

Efficient custom operators are essential for modern deep learning
workloads, yet developing high-performance kernels for Ascend NPUs
remains slow, expert-intensive, and difficult to automate. Although AI
agents now approach expert performance on GPU kernel benchmarks, current
models remain less capable of generating AscendC kernels for NPUs,
potentially reflecting the relative scarcity of relevant training data.
We thus present CAKE, a CANN-native system for deployable custom
operators that combines adaptive multi-DSL routing, separate Generation
and Evolution modes, and reviewed knowledge reuse through CAKE Book and
a Self-Evolving Agent. On 53 CANN-Bench v1.1 operators on Ascend 950PR,
CAKE’s aggregated results achieve $`100\%`$ case pass rate on the
standard set (1,060/1,060) and $`98.28\%`$ on the hidden set
(4,167/4,240), with an overall mean score of 78.63 out of 100 and an
average performance speedup of $`1.334\times`$ over the baseline.
Evolution then pushes correct operators further: EngramGateFusion cuts
aggregate device time by $`46.6\%`$ over 20 rounds and roughly halves
the mean roofline gap. These results offer a practical path toward
closing Ascend’s AI-for-kernel capability gap.

## 1 Motivation and System Overview

An accelerator reaches its advertised throughput only when every
operator in a model is backed by an efficient, hardware-tuned compute
kernel. Kernel quality, not a chip’s peak throughput, sets end-to-end
performance, and writing these kernels by hand is slow and demands
scarce low-level expertise. Automating that work has become an active
research target.

Large language models have made that target newly reachable: coupled
with execution feedback and search, they can generate correct and
competitive GPU kernels. This progress rests on a favorable ecosystem.
CUDA and Triton expose abundant open kernels, documented optimization
idioms, and large public code corpora, so a model can recognize and
adapt patterns it has effectively already seen. NPUs such as Ascend
offer no comparable foundation; their vendor programming model, AscendC,
appears only sparsely in public data. In published evaluations,
general-purpose models succeed on essentially _none_ of the complex
AscendC kernels they attempt in a zero-shot setting \[[1](#bib.bib1)\],
and one-shot AscendC pass rates remain at or below $`2.1\%`$ where CUDA
reaches $`44.2`$–$`52.6\%`$ \[[2](#bib.bib2), [3](#bib.bib3)\]. These
results motivate supplementing pretrained models with Ascend-specific
programming knowledge and execution feedback.

Ascend kernel development requires coordinating heterogeneous compute
units over an explicitly managed on-chip memory hierarchy, with data
movement, pipeline overlap, and synchronization all under program
control
(Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Ascend 950 Vector: Regbase SIMD and SIMT ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
describes the additional programming paths on Ascend 950). The
consequence for a code-generating agent is that an Ascend operator is
not a single kernel but a *two-part artifact* \[[3](#bib.bib3)\]: a
host-side tiling program that decides how data are partitioned and
moved, and a device-side kernel that decides how computation is
scheduled. Performance is a property of the coordination between these
two components: tiling determines the data available to each core, while
the device kernel schedules computation and transfers.

In practice the bar is higher still. The unit an engineer can actually
ship is neither a host program nor a device kernel in isolation, but a
_deployable CANN custom operator_: one that builds, packages, installs,
binds to Python, passes precision checks against a reference, and
profiles on real hardware. Recent Ascend systems each automate one slice
of this chain
(Section [1.1](#S1.SS1 "1.1 Related Systems ‣ 1 Motivation and System Overview ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
and
Table [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Motivation and System Overview ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU"))—training
a model, transcompiling a domain-specific language (DSL), optimizing an
existing kernel, or supplying curated domain knowledge to an
evolutionary search. The last of these, AgenticCANN, is the closest
prior system to ours and the one that most directly confronts the corpus
problem: it organizes AscendC expertise into a six-level taxonomy, from
hardware mental model down to verified kernel exemplars, and injects the
levels selectively by evolutionary phase, raising the share of
elementwise kernels it can synthesize from $`57\%`$ to $`86\%`$ on
Ascend 910B \[[4](#bib.bib4)\]. This demonstrates the value of explicit
domain knowledge. Its reported feasibility also varies by operator
family: $`90`$–$`100\%`$ on elementwise and normalization operators, but
$`56\%`$ on fusion, over a private $`54`$-operator sample.

These results motivate a workflow that carries generated code through
packaging and deployment while reusing the results of previous runs.
Such a workflow needs to retain intermediate artifacts for debugging,
use evaluation outcomes to guide generation, and make useful lessons
available to later tasks.

We present CANNBot-CAKE (hereafter CAKE), an open-source CANN-native
agentic workflow released in CANNBot, Huawei’s official repository for
Ascend agents.¹¹ 1
[https://gitcode.com/cann/cannbot-skills](https://gitcode.com/cann/cannbot-skills)
CAKE generates and evolves deployable Ascend operators from either a
natural-language requirement or an existing AscendC baseline. CAKE uses
existing language models to coordinate these stages. A request becomes
an operator contract, then a PyTorch reference, a functional form, a
routed DSL baseline, host-side tiling, device AscendC code, a CANN
package, a Python binding, and an evaluation record—each a durable
object that can be inspected, validated, and reused. A multi-DSL
_router_ chooses among four code-generation tracks using the operator’s
structural features and previous evaluation scores. It also explores
less-tested tracks that may perform better. Generation mode produces one
deployable operator through generation, validation, and repair. A
profiling assistant, the _Advisor_, diagnoses performance bottlenecks
and suggests changes. Evolution mode (CAKE-evo) runs a multi-round
campaign that reuses shared artifacts, spawns isolated variants, and
ranks them by compilation, precision, and performance. Candidates are
scored by automated evaluation on CAKE-Bench, a user-defined evaluation
suite that we instantiate with the official CANN-Bench task
set \[[5](#bib.bib5)\]; a _self-evolving agent_ mines those measured
runs to improve the router, skills, and repair templates; and a
cross-user knowledge base, CAKE Book, accumulates verified lessons in
interlinked wiki pages \[[6](#bib.bib6)\].

Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Motivation and System Overview ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
summarizes five components of CAKE. First, a CANN-native staged pipeline
(CAKE-Agents) turns operator intent into a deployable custom operator
through Generation and Evolution modes, exposing every stage—contract,
reference, DSL, host tiling, kernel, package, binding, and evaluation—as
an inspectable object. Second, the CAKE-Router makes DSL choice an
explicit, measured decision over four code-generation tracks: a
capability gate removes infeasible track–chip–operator-type
combinations, a per-track item-response model turns past evaluated
operators into ability estimates adjusted for operator difficulty, and
an information-gated exploration rule allocates additional evaluations
to tracks that could overtake the incumbent
(Section [3](#S3 "3 Adaptive Routing and Generation ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")).
Third, a Skills harness of more than thirty typed lifecycle tools—for
description, lowering, optimization, evaluation, and debugging—gives the
agents a reusable substrate for operator engineering
(Section [2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 The Skills harness ‣ 2 From Intent to Deployable Operator ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")).
Fourth, CAKE Book accumulates verified CANN experience as a cross-user
wiki, shared and updated across users and agents and queried before
generation. Fifth, a self-evolving agent closes the loop: continuous
automated evaluation on CAKE-Bench produces measured signals that an
analysis module mines to trace, judge, and edit skills and to promote
evidence-gated improvements back into the router, prompts, repair
templates, and CAKE Book. The evidence in this report combines
aggregated standard- and hidden-set results on 53 CANN-Bench operators
on Ascend 950PR, replayable Router decisions, and operational evidence
from the CAKE Book write path. The EngramGateFusion case study
demonstrates multi-round optimization of a generated kernel.
Section [7](#S7 "7 Scope and Future Directions ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
outlines further development of the workflow and its evaluation.

Table [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Motivation and System Overview ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
contrasts CAKE with the closest Ascend-native systems by their
generation, optimization, delivery, and knowledge-reuse mechanisms.

### 1.1 Related Systems

#### Kernel benchmarks and feedback-driven kernel agents.

Benchmarks such as KernelBench, TritonBench, and MultiKernelBench
reframed kernel synthesis around measured compile, correctness, and
performance funnels \[[8](#bib.bib8), [9](#bib.bib9), [2](#bib.bib2)\],
and a wave of GPU kernel agents—among them KernelAgent, CudaForge,
AutoKernel, KernelFoundry, and KernelEvolve—showed that hardware
feedback and search drive synthesis past one-shot
prompting \[[10](#bib.bib10), [11](#bib.bib11), [12](#bib.bib12),
[13](#bib.bib13), [14](#bib.bib14)\]. On Ascend, related systems use
several approaches to supply domain expertise. AscendKernelGen trains a
domain-adapted model on a reasoning dataset to emit AscendC
code \[[1](#bib.bib1)\]; AscendCraft transcompiles a lightweight DSL
into AscendC through constrained lowering passes \[[7](#bib.bib7)\];
AscendOptimizer improves an already correct AscendC implementation
through rewind-distilled experience and tiling
search \[[3](#bib.bib3)\]; and AgenticCANN attacks the corpus scarcity
head-on, encoding AscendC expertise as a six-level taxonomy—hardware
model, math-to-code mapping, execution invariants, tiling formulas, API
signatures, verified exemplars—and admitting different levels at
different phases of an evolutionary search, while scheduling
high-exploration agents for seed discovery and cheaper agents for
refinement \[[4](#bib.bib4)\]. Its ablations measure the contribution of
this knowledge: adding knowledge levels lifts elementwise feasibility
from $`57\%`$ to $`86\%`$, with hardware-constraint knowledge alone
worth $`20`$ percentage points on LayerNorm. The difference relevant to
CAKE is how this knowledge is maintained. AgenticCANN uses an
expert-curated taxonomy; CAKE Book also collects entries from measured
runs and promotes them only after cross-user review and on-device
verification, which is what allows later operators to benefit from
earlier failures.
Table [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Motivation and System Overview ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
compares these systems’ delivery scope; CAKE targets the chain from
intent to a deployable, benchmark-validated operator.

#### Routing.

Learned routers such as RouteLLM dispatch a query to a stronger or
weaker model \[[15](#bib.bib15)\], and compiler auto-schedulers such as
Ansor use learned cost models to select a schedule within a single
intermediate representation \[[16](#bib.bib16)\]. Kernel-generation
agents, by contrast, are largely single-DSL \[[7](#bib.bib7),
[1](#bib.bib1), [11](#bib.bib11)\]; the few that span several backends
either expose support for multiple DSLs without a published selection
rule or defer the choice to an opaque per-kernel agent
decision \[[17](#bib.bib17), [12](#bib.bib12)\]. CAKE instead scores
four peer code-generation tracks under a published rule: an
item-response model estimates each track’s ability per structural
dimension from past evaluated operators, so that the ordering of tracks
changes with the operator rather than being fixed, and every decision is
recorded with the candidate estimates that produced it
(Section [3](#S3 "3 Adaptive Routing and Generation ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")).

#### Agent memory and knowledge bases.

Agent memory has progressed from per-episode
self-reflection \[[18](#bib.bib18)\] and single-agent skill or
experience libraries \[[19](#bib.bib19), [20](#bib.bib20)\] to
self-linking memory notes \[[21](#bib.bib21)\], and recently to sharing
across actors through banked lessons for cooperating code
agents \[[22](#bib.bib22)\] and provenance-tracked multi-user
memory \[[23](#bib.bib23)\]. In the same Ascend domain, AscendOptimizer
mines a single-agent experience bank for kernel
rewriting \[[3](#bib.bib3)\], and AgenticCANN supplies a hand-authored
taxonomy of AscendC knowledge as retrieval context \[[4](#bib.bib4)\].
CAKE Book combines three properties: it is an agent-maintained wiki of
interlinked pages with an explicit error notebook rather than a flat
store; it is written by the runs it serves, so its contents grow with
measured evidence rather than with expert authoring effort; and its
entries become canonical only after cross-user, human review and
on-device verification.

#### Self-evolving agents.

A growing body of work studies agents that improve themselves: recursive
self-referential systems rewrite their own
scaffolding \[[24](#bib.bib24), [25](#bib.bib25)\], automated
agent-design methods search the space of agentic
architectures \[[26](#bib.bib26)\], and evolutionary approaches maintain
populations of self-modifying agents validated by benchmark
fitness \[[27](#bib.bib27)\]. In the kernel domain, agentic systems
evolve archives of optimized kernels \[[28](#bib.bib28)\]. CAKE’s
Self-Evolving Agent targets the generation workflow. It mines many
completed generation and profiling runs to promote evidence-gated
improvements into the router, skills, repair templates, and CAKE Book.

## 2 From Intent to Deployable Operator

CAKE divides operator development into stages with explicit inputs,
outputs, and validation checks. Each stage produces an artifact used by
subsequent stages, allowing failures to be diagnosed before the workflow
proceeds.

- •
  Operator contract generation. The request (or an api_description.md)
  is compiled into an _operator contract_ (op_desc.json): the single
  source of truth for the operator’s identity, semantic formulas,
  representative I/O with dtype/shape constraints, attributes, and case
  table. Every later stage derives its signature from it, including the
  schema features that are otherwise lost downstream — is_list,
  optional, string-attribute enums, output_shape derivations, and
  channel-first layout.
- •
  Reference and functional forms. CAKE builds a PyTorch reference,
  preserving a supplied implementation verbatim and fixing random seeds
  for reproducibility. It then converts the reference to a stateless
  module_fn. The reference defines expected outputs for correctness
  checks, the test inputs exercise both reference and generated code,
  and the functional form exposes dataflow for routing and lowering.
- •
  Multi-DSL router. The router represents the contract and functional
  form as an eight-dimensional structural profile, removes tracks that
  cannot support the operator type or target device, and scores the
  remaining tracks using previous evaluations.
  Section [3](#S3 "3 Adaptive Routing and Generation ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
  describes the model. Users can instead specify a track directly
  through the contract’s dsl_track field.
- •
  Lowering and project construction. The selected track lowers the
  functional form into host-side tiling and device-side code while
  preserving the contract as the interface authority. CAKE materializes
  the generated source, build configuration, tiling metadata, wrappers,
  and project skeleton as separate artifacts so that a failure can be
  localized to a stage rather than attributed to an opaque model
  response.
- •
  Package, install, and bind. A candidate is built as a CANN
  custom-operator package, installed into the pinned environment, and
  exposed through the generated Python binding. These stages are part of
  the deliverable rather than post-processing: code that compiles as a
  kernel snippet but cannot be packaged or invoked does not count as a
  completed operator.
- •
  Evaluate and repair. The installed operator is executed against the
  reference under dtype-aware precision checks and on-device timing.
  Compilation, packaging, binding, correctness, and profiling results
  are written next to the candidate. The resulting evidence routes the
  next action: build failures return to lowering or project
  construction, numerical failures return to the contract, reference, or
  tiling assumptions, and correct but slow candidates enter
  profiling-guided repair or Evolution mode.

The unit of progress in this lifecycle is therefore an artifact plus its
validation record. A run can stop at a failed intermediate stage without
losing the evidence needed to diagnose it, while a successful run leaves
a package, binding, test record, profile, and provenance trail that
another engineer or agent can inspect. These records support both
optimization within the current run and knowledge reuse across runs.

### 2.1 The Skills harness

The stages above describe what is produced; the Skills harness is what
executes them. A skill is a typed lifecycle tool: it names the artifact
it consumes, the artifact it writes, and the condition under which its
output is admissible. The orchestrating agent does not contain the
procedures — it declares the skills it may call, currently more than
thirty, and the runtime resolves each call against that declaration.
Adding a capability therefore means adding a skill and listing it, not
editing the agent.

The harness coordinates skill selection, validation, and failure
recovery.

#### Stage binding, with track-specific variants.

Skills are bound to stages rather than invoked ad hoc. Contract,
reference, functional conversion, and tiling pre-classification are
shared by every run; the router then selects a code-generation track,
and the lowering stages dispatch to the variant of each skill
specialized for that track — separate lowering and call-generation
skills exist for the Vector and the fused Cube–Vector paths, so that the
difference between them lives in the harness rather than inside a
branching prompt. Review, evaluation, Advisor-guided repair, and run
retrospective are shared again. A track is thus a path through a fixed
skill graph, which is why the router’s choice is auditable after the
fact.

#### Stage validation.

A stage advances only when its artifact passes a machine-checked gate.
The contract illustrates these checks: before any code is generated, the
op_desc is checked for dtype coverage against the full case table, for
signature agreement with the task’s declared schema, and for the shape
metadata that packaging later depends on. These checks catch incomplete
dtype coverage, argument mismatches, and missing output-shape metadata
before they propagate to compilation or packaging. A failed check
returns control to the stage that produced the artifact.

#### Execution tracing and failure recovery.

Two cross-cutting skills record execution and coordinate repairs
throughout a run. Every skill call is bracketed by a trace record, so a
run leaves a complete, machine-readable account of which skills fired,
in what order, and with what outcome — this trace is the input the
self-evolving agent of
Section [5](#S5 "5 CAKE Book and System-Level Self-Evolution ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
reads to identify recurring skill failures. Alongside it, a test-driven
meta-skill governs what happens on failure: a diagnosis is treated as a
hypothesis that stays open until an end-to-end pass closes it, and a
failure mode seen twice must be pushed back into the lowering step or
the project skeleton that permitted it rather than accumulated as
another entry in a pitfall list. Retries are bounded, and a stage that
does not pass its gate produces no commit, so the version history
records the stages that cleared their checks.

## 3 Adaptive Routing and Generation

CAKE carries four code-generation _tracks_ that can each produce a
deployable operator: DSL-A, the mature AscendC-lowering track that
covers both vector and cube–vector operators on the 910 series; DSL-B, a
high-level tile DSL whose strength is cube–vector topology; DSL-C, the
vector and cube–vector generation track for the 950; and the SIMT track
detailed in
Appendix [A.5](#A1.SS5 "A.5 SIMT code generation ‣ Appendix A Ascend 950 Vector: Regbase SIMD and SIMT ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU").
A track is an _implementation route_, not an operator class: whether an
operator is vector, cube–vector, or SIMT-shaped is an input to the
routing decision, and several tracks compete for the same class.

Track performance depends on both the operator’s structure and the
current code-generation skills. A track that works well for one operator
family may perform poorly on another, and skill updates can change this
relationship. CAKE therefore estimates track suitability from previous
evaluations. The router has four components
(Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ The routing loop. ‣ 3 Adaptive Routing and Generation ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")):
a feasibility gate, a feature extractor, a scoring layer, and an
append-only observation ledger.

#### L0: feasibility gate.

A declared capability table marks each (track, chip, operator type)
triple feasible or not, and infeasible tracks are removed before any
scoring happens. This prevents attempts on unsupported configurations.
Forward binary compatibility widens the declared set (a track feasible
on 910B is feasible on 910C). On the 950, only DSL-C is feasible for
vector and cube–vector operators, so those operators land on DSL-C
without any scoring; and the SIMT track exclusively owns the SIMT
operator type, which no other track accepts, so the two never compete.
When the gate leaves nothing feasible, the router _abstains_: it emits
no decision and hands the model the full track menu with each track’s
skills. Abstention has two causes that are reported separately — an
unrecognized device string, so that no gate can be applied at all, and a
recognized device on which the requested operator type has no feasible
track.

#### L1: operator features and difficulty.

The contract and the functional form are reduced to an eight-dimensional
feature vector $`\varphi`$ over the dimensions $`(T,S,B,R,D,M,F,C)`$ —
tiling structure, scheduling depth, blocking, reduction, dtype and
quantization spread, data movement and irregular access, fusion breadth,
and cube intensity. Operators already characterized in the library get
an exact vector derived from their reference AST; new operators get a
heuristic vector, which is the normal case in production. A scalar
difficulty follows from a calibrated weight vector $`\beta`$,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
b\;=\;\beta^{\top}\varphi,\qquad\beta=(0.51,\,0.78,\,0.59,\,0.70,\,0.44,\,0.61,\,0.64,\,0.98),
``` |  | (1) |

pinned to a feature-specification version so that difficulty stays
comparable across recalibrations. Crucially $`b`$ is a property of the
operator, not of the track, which is what makes the routing decision
robust to noise in a heuristic $`\varphi`$: in the scalar regime below,
$`b`$ cancels when tracks are compared.

#### L2: track ability and the routing score.

Raw mean scores are difficult to compare when tracks have attempted
different operator sets. On the current corpus DSL-A’s mean achieved
score is $`0.576`$ against DSL-C’s $`0.471`$, a gap that would read as a
clear ordering; the ability estimates below put them at
$`-0.95\pm 0.38`$ and $`-0.99\pm 0.36`$, statistically indistinguishable
under this model. The raw $`0.105`$ difference alone therefore does not
establish a track-ability advantage.

CAKE therefore estimates a per-track ability $`\theta`$ under a
continuous item-response model. One observation is a completed
generation-and-evaluation run: a track attempted an operator of known
difficulty $`b`$ and achieved a normalized score $`y\in[0,1]`$. The link
is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[\,y\mid\theta,b\,]\;=\;\sigma(\theta-b),\qquad\sigma(x)=\bigl(1+e^{-x}\bigr)^{-1},
``` |  | (2) |

with a beta likelihood on the continuous score and a posterior over
$`\theta`$ obtained by expected-a-posteriori integration against an
$`\mathcal{N}(0,1)`$ prior on a fixed grid. Because $`b`$ is computable
from $`\varphi`$ before any observation exists
(Equation [1](#S3.E1 "In L1: operator features and difficulty. ‣ 3 Adaptive Routing and Generation ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")),
the router can assign an initial score to a track with no history using
the prior. Such a score reflects prior assumptions rather than measured
track performance.

A single scalar $`\theta`$ per track is not enough. With scalar
abilities the comparison $`\sigma(\theta_{t}-b)`$ ranks tracks
identically for every operator, since $`b`$ is shared — the router would
degenerate into a fixed preference order. CAKE therefore fits a
per-dimension ability model per track: writing
$`z=\operatorname{logit}(y)+b`$, a ridge-regularized weighted least
squares (intercept unpenalized) gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
z\;\approx\;a_{0}\;+\;\sum_{d}\theta_{d}\cdot\frac{\varphi_{d}}{3},\qquad p_{\text{track}}(\varphi)\;=\;\sigma\!\Bigl(a_{0}+\sum_{d}\theta_{d}\frac{\varphi_{d}}{3}-b\Bigr),
``` |  | (3) |

where $`a_{0}`$ is the track’s overall ability on the same scale as the
scalar $`\theta`$ and $`\theta_{d}`$ is its ability increment on
dimension $`d`$. The interaction terms $`\theta_{d}\varphi_{d}`$ are
what make the ranking operator-dependent. Fitting requires at least as
many valid observations as free parameters; below that threshold the
router falls back to the scalar form and records the fallback in its
decision log.
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ The routing loop. ‣ 3 Adaptive Routing and Generation ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
shows the fitted profiles: the three DSL tracks are close on tiling,
reduction, and dtype handling, and separate sharply on data movement
($`M`$) and blocking ($`B`$).

#### A worked decision.

Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ The routing loop. ‣ 3 Adaptive Routing and Generation ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
traces four operators through
Equation [3](#S3.E3 "In L2: track ability and the routing score. ‣ 3 Adaptive Routing and Generation ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
on the 910B. The first pair illustrates how operator features change the
selected track. gelu and gather are both vector operators with the same
feasible track set and similar difficulty ($`b=-2.18`$ against $`-1.40`$
after centering). Their feature vectors differ in data movement, where
$`\varphi_{M}`$ goes from $`0`$ to $`2`$, and dtype spread, where
$`\varphi_{D}`$ goes from $`2`$ to $`1`$. The larger between-track
contrast is in data movement: DSL-A’s $`\theta_{M}`$ is $`-1.69`$ while
DSL-C’s is $`-0.31`$. As a result, DSL-A’s lead on gelu ($`0.694`$
against $`0.613`$) becomes a deficit on gather ($`0.239`$ against
$`0.366`$), and the decision flips. The remaining two rows show two
further dimensions taking control: conv_2d has $`\varphi_{B}=3`$ and
goes to DSL-B, whose $`\theta_{B}=+2.83`$ is the largest single
coefficient in the model; mha carries $`\varphi_{S}=3`$ and returns to
DSL-A on scheduling depth, where $`\theta_{S}=+2.45`$ against DSL-C’s
$`+0.91`$ is the largest per-dimension difference in DSL-A’s favour.
Reduction works the other way, since DSL-C’s $`\theta_{R}=+2.75`$
exceeds DSL-A’s $`+2.26`$. DSL-A wins even though mha’s centered
difficulty is $`+7.57`$ and every track’s predicted normalized score is
low. The four examples select three different tracks despite using the
same device and fitted track profiles.

#### Evaluation ledger and skill versions.

The observation ledger is append-only and grows one row per evaluated
operator: the track used, the device, the difficulty and feature vector,
the achieved normalized score, and a fingerprint of the code-generation
skills that produced it. Any evaluation harness that returns a
per-operator score on a comparable scale can supply $`y`$ — CAKE-Bench’s
per-operator score is one such source, a user’s own metric is another.
This allows new operator evaluations to update the router without
rerunning a fixed benchmark suite. Observations flagged as
infrastructure failures, as reward-hacking candidates, or as internally
inconsistent submissions are retained in the ledger but excluded from
ability estimation. To account for changes in code-generation skills,
the router identifies each track configuration by the pair (track,
skill_version): observations from a superseded skill version enter
estimation at half weight, which widens the posterior and prompts
re-measurement of the updated track. New evaluations receive full
weight.

#### Selecting tracks for exploration.

Testing a track requires a full generation, build, and evaluation cycle.
CAKE limits these additional evaluations using two criteria. A
Bernoulli-style information proxy $`I=p(1-p)`$ at the current estimate
is the *eligibility* heuristic. For the continuous scores modeled here,
this is not the Fisher information of the beta likelihood. An optimistic
upper bound $`\theta+1.96\,\mathrm{se}`$ identifies tracks that could
outperform the currently preferred track. Among eligible alternatives,
the router selects the one with the highest upper bound. Thus, the
information proxy controls eligibility, while the upper bound determines
which alternative to test. Ranking by the information proxy alone would
instead favor scores near $`0.5`$, where $`p(1-p)`$ is largest.

After a skill update, the router compares how many current-version
evaluations are available for each track. Tracks with fewer observations
than their peers receive a re-measurement bonus. If all tracks are
equally under-sampled, no differential bonus is applied; the ordinary
eligibility and upper-bound criteria still govern exploration.

#### The routing loop.

Each completed evaluation updates the evidence used for subsequent
routing. At the routing stage the router writes its decision next to the
operator’s artifacts, together with the full candidate snapshot — every
feasible track’s ability estimate, predicted normalized score,
information proxy, and skill fingerprint. At the evaluation stage the
achieved score is written back as a new observation, the affected
track’s posterior moves, and the next operator of similar character may
route differently. Both events are also appended to a central timeline,
which also records abstentions and routing errors. The saved features,
scores, and skill versions allow a past decision to be reconstructed
using the information available at the time.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## 4 Evolutionary Optimization

Generation mode provides a working implementation that can serve as the
starting point for performance optimization. Evolution mode, or
CAKE-evo, explores tiling, buffering, and fusion choices through
parallel candidate generation and on-device evaluation. Profiling
identifies the bottlenecks to target in each round.

### 4.1 Profiling-driven analysis layer

Before generating variants, CAKE-evo estimates a performance ceiling
from the input shapes and dtypes, device clock, HBM/L2 bandwidth, and
peak cube/vector throughput. Following a roofline decomposition, the
modeled lower-bound execution time is the maximum of four pipeline
times,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
T_{\min}\;=\;\max\bigl(t_{\text{hbm\_read}},\;t_{\text{write}},\;t_{\text{cube}},\;t_{\text{vector}}\bigr),
``` |  | (4) |

where reads and writes are treated as separate channels that overlap.
For $`b_{\text{out}}`$ output bytes, writes follow an L2-fill-first
model: traffic up to the L2 capacity $`C_{L2}`$ uses bandwidth
$`\beta_{L2}`$, and the remainder uses HBM bandwidth
$`\beta_{\text{HBM}}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
t_{\text{write}}=\begin{cases}b_{\text{out}}/\beta_{L2}&b_{\text{out}}\leq C_{L2}\\[2.0pt]
C_{L2}/\beta_{L2}+(b_{\text{out}}-C_{L2})/\beta_{\text{HBM}}&b_{\text{out}}>C_{L2}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (5) |

The dominant term in
Eq. ([4](#S4.E4 "In 4.1 Profiling-driven analysis layer ‣ 4 Evolutionary Optimization ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU"))
is the *bottleneck signature* (memory vs. compute, and which pipe), and
the arithmetic intensity $`\mathrm{AI}=\text{FLOPs}/\text{bytes}`$
versus the ridge point $`\beta_{\text{HBM}}^{-1}\!\cdot\!\text{peak}`$
confirms the regime. A complementary *fusion analysis* parses the
operator’s dataflow graph and flags intermediates that would otherwise
be materialized to HBM, quantifying the traffic a loop fusion would
save. Together these yield, per case: (i) a *ceiling-derived target*
$`T_{\min}`$ that replaces a hand-picked speedup goal, (ii) a bottleneck
label that selects which optimization family to try, and (iii) a loop
fusion recommendation.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 4: Roofline ceiling model
(Eq. [4](#S4.E4 "In 4.1 Profiling-driven analysis layer ‣ 4 Evolutionary Optimization ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")).
Each case is placed by its arithmetic intensity (AI); the binding
pipeline gives the roof $`T_{\min}`$, and the *headroom* (gap from the
measured point up to the roof) bounds how much evolution can still gain.
A variant that reaches its roof ($`\text{headroom}\!\approx\!1`$) is
converged.

The resulting $`T_{\min}`$ is an optimistic analytical floor under the
assumed overlap and traffic model, not a measured attainable latency.
Dependencies, contention, and instruction overhead can keep a correct
kernel above this floor even when further optimization is ineffective.
We define *headroom* as the measured runtime divided by $`T_{\min}`$; a
value near one indicates little remaining improvement under this model.

### 4.2 The evolutionary loop

Each round
(Fig. [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.2 The evolutionary loop ‣ 4 Evolutionary Optimization ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU"))
generates $`N`$ variants in parallel, assigning each an optimization
direction based on the identified bottleneck. For example, a
memory-bound chain may benefit from fusion, while a compute-bound kernel
may benefit from different tiling or instruction scheduling. Candidates
are compiled, evaluated, ranked by speedup, and grouped into good,
medium, and poor tiers. The next round samples implementations from
these tiers as starting points.

During advisor-in-the-loop consultation (AIC), the Advisor examines the
profile of the best candidate and supplies bottleneck-specific
suggestions for the next round. The search stops when the measured
runtime approaches the modeled floor ($`\text{headroom}\!\approx\!1`$,
Fig. [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Profiling-driven analysis layer ‣ 4 Evolutionary Optimization ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU"))
or the round budget is exhausted. Post-evolution mining (PMR) then
extracts validated optimizations as candidate rules for reuse on other
operators.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 5: The CAKE-evo loop. The analysis layer (blue) sets the ceiling
target and bottleneck-driven variant assignment; the evolutionary stages
(green) spawn, measure, and tier variants; AIC injects
profiling-grounded guidance; the roofline headroom provides the stop
test; PMR compounds knowledge into rules.

### 4.3 Strategy knowledge

Optimization directions are drawn from a curated strategy library
derived from production operators and organized into five classes
(Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Strategy knowledge ‣ 4 Evolutionary Optimization ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")).
The kernel-level classes cover dtype handling (D), performance (P), and
numerical accuracy (A). Fusion strategies (F) eliminate intermediate
global-memory transfers; host-level strategies (H) select specialized
kernels and distribute work across cores according to input shapes.

| Class | Scope |  Representative strategies |
|----|----|----|
| D  Multi-dtype | kernel |  mixed precision; template / TilingKey dtype dispatch |
| P  Performance | kernel |  double buffering; adaptive tiling; pipeline sync; 32B alignment; vectorized copy; matmul scheduling; L1/L2 cache hierarchy |
| A  Accuracy | kernel |  FP32 intermediate; Welford mean/var; rounding mode; softmax stability; high-precision rsqrt |
| F  Fusion | cross-op |  elementwise-chain anti-spill; norm$`+`$epilogue; matmul$`+`$epilogue (CV) |
| H  Host-level | host |  TilingKey priority-chain dispatch; multi-core load balance; L2/L1 memory tiering |

Table 3: Strategy classes. D/P/A are kernel-level; F and H raise the
altitude to cross-operator fusion and host-side, shape-driven dispatch.

Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.3 Strategy knowledge ‣ 4 Evolutionary Optimization ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
maps profiling results to candidate strategies. Inputs include the
dominant pipeline in
Eq. [4](#S4.E4 "In 4.1 Profiling-driven analysis layer ‣ 4 Evolutionary Optimization ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU"),
opportunities to fuse intermediate operations, and differences in
bottlenecks across input shapes. Assigning variants different applicable
strategies lets a round test several responses to the measured
bottleneck.

| Bottleneck signature |  Routed strategies |
|----|----|
| memory-bound $`+`$ fusable chain |  Fusion to keep intermediates off GMEM; double buffering; alignment; vectorized copy; memory-tier selection |
| compute-bound (vector) |  Adaptive tiling; small-dimension row merging; algorithm selection; FP32 intermediates where precision requires them |
| compute-bound (cube) |  Matmul scheduling (SplitK/StreamK); L1/L2 cache optimization; matmul-epilogue fusion |
| instruction / scalar-bound |  Algorithm redesign; specialized AscendC APIs; narrow synchronization |
| load imbalance (straggler core) |  Host-side dispatch and multi-core load balancing |
| shape regimes diverge across cases |  Multiple TilingKeys with a specialized kernel per shape regime |

Table 4: Bottleneck-signature $`\rightarrow`$ strategy routing across
the classes in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Strategy knowledge ‣ 4 Evolutionary Optimization ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU").
The roofline verdict and fusion analysis select which optimization
family each variant explores.

Finally, the library is not static: the PMR step
(Fig. [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.2 The evolutionary loop ‣ 4 Evolutionary Optimization ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU"))
distills the optimizations that were *validated* to improve performance
during evolution into reusable rules, so each optimized kernel improves
both the strategy set and the routing table for the next.

### 4.4 Case study: evolving EngramGateFusion without an official kernel baseline

EngramGateFusion is a CANN-Bench level-3 operator that combines a
per-step gated recurrence with a dilated depthwise convolution. The
benchmark specifies the mathematical contract and a correctness
reference, but provides no official optimized kernel. A conventional
speedup against a vendor implementation is therefore unavailable. We
instead use three anchors: CAKE-evo’s first working kernel, the unfused
PyTorch composition (roughly one hundred small-operator launches), and
the case-specific hardware lower bound $`T_{\min}`$ from
Eq. ([4](#S4.E4 "In 4.1 Profiling-driven analysis layer ‣ 4 Evolutionary Optimization ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")).
The campaign covers 20 shape configurations and two bf16 outputs; the
final package passes all 20 official grading cases. Development and
round-to-round timing used Ascend910B2, while official grading used
Ascend 910C.

For round $`r`$ and case $`i`$, the campaign reports the fusion
indicator $`S_{r}=\frac{1}{20}\sum_{i}t_{\mathrm{eager},i}/t_{r,i}`$ and
the roofline gap $`G_{r}=\frac{1}{20}\sum_{i}t_{r,i}/T_{\min,i}`$. A
larger $`S_{r}`$ indicates that the fused kernel increasingly amortizes
the unfused composition, while a smaller $`G_{r}`$ indicates movement
toward the hardware floor. The two ratios have different evidentiary
roles: $`G_{r}`$ compares device times directly, whereas $`S_{r}`$
divides end-to-end eager wall time by device-only kernel time and is
thus a round-to-round fusion indicator, not a same-basis end-to-end
speedup.
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.4 Case study: evolving EngramGateFusion without an official kernel baseline ‣ 4 Evolutionary Optimization ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
shows the evolution trajectory, with endpoint roofline gaps, per-round
LLM calls, and annotations of the main optimization steps.

![Refer to caption]()

Figure 6: EngramGateFusion evolution over 20 CAKE-evo rounds and 20
CANN-Bench cases. The line is the mean fusion indicator against the
unfused PyTorch composition (left axis); gray bars show LLM calls in
each round (right axis), and warm-colored callouts identify the
mechanisms behind the largest gains. The indicator rises from
$`45.5\times`$ to $`98.2\times`$, while the endpoint annotations show
the mean kernel-to-roofline ratio falling from $`25.7\times`$ to
$`12.6\times`$. Because the line mixes eager wall time with device
kernel time, it is used only as a trajectory indicator; a separate
same-basis measurement gives a final mean end-to-end speedup of
$`29.5\times`$ (geometric mean $`27.6\times`$). Round 20 performed
verification, packaging, and a device-fault fix and therefore has calls
but no new performance point; the dashed segment repeats the round-19
value and does not represent a new timing measurement.

Across the 20 cases, aggregate device time falls from $`1451.7\,\mu`$s
for the round-1 kernel to $`775.7\,\mu`$s in round 19, a $`46.6\%`$
reduction or $`1.87\times`$ within-system speedup. The local score rises
from 64.53 to 72.80; the packaged kernel scores 71.30 on the official
grader with all 20 cases passing. The precision report records
bit-identical agreement on six cases and at most one bf16 unit in the
last place (ULP) on the remainder. The timing improvement is measured
against CAKE’s round-1 kernel on the same development device. The
campaign reached its 20-round budget, not the roofline stopping
threshold.

The local and official scores are not directly comparable: the
development device has 48 vector cores and the grading device has 40,
which also changes shape-dependent dispatch. Round acceptance used a
local oracle rather than the official grading path. The first official
submission failed 12 cases because host-side UB accounting diverged from
the kernel layout on the grading device. Round 20 fixed this by deriving
both layouts from a shared header; the final 20/20 result refers to the
repaired package, not every intermediate candidate.

The performance gains followed several revisions to the agent’s
bottleneck analysis. In round 2, measurements showed that the fixed
issue overhead of a vector API call dominated its length-dependent cost,
making call reduction a priority. In round 3, processing sequence
positions by their index modulo the dilation factor reduced the
convolution ring buffer from $`K`$ times the dilation factor to $`K`$
rows, where $`K`$ is the number of convolution taps.

Middle rounds introduced double buffering in the Unified Buffer (UB) and
shape-aware host tiling. The agent also revised its interpretation of
three-source vector instructions: replacing a chain of simpler
operations with one multiply-add could reduce instruction issue
overhead. Later rounds tested combinations of changes and revised a
code-size rule that had rejected useful candidates. In round 19, folding
conv_norm_weight into the convolution tap weights removed a
multiplication from each row. The complete campaign used 36 generated
variants and 1,037 LLM calls across 20 rounds; 186 of those calls belong
to the final verification-and-packaging round. The resulting
measurements and successful changes provide material for post-evolution
mining (PMR): instruction-cost estimates, conditions under which a rule
fails, and combinations of optimizations that can be tested on other
operators.

## 5 CAKE Book and System-Level Self-Evolution

Evolution mode improves one operator implementation by searching over
candidate variants under a fixed operator contract. CAKE also contains a
system-level improvement loop whose target is the generator itself. This
loop is implemented by two cooperating components: CAKE Book, an LLM
Wiki-based agentic knowledge-management system, and the Self-Evolving
Agent, a persistent AI agent that monitors CAKE runs and turns observed
engineering experience into human-reviewed improvements. Together they
make CAKE less dependent on a single model’s prior knowledge:
compilation failures, profiling signals, successful optimizations, and
human corrections become reusable system memory.

### 5.1 CAKE Book as Agent-Native Reference

CAKE Book is the knowledge layer used by CAKE agents before, during, and
after operator generation. Following the open-source LLM Wiki pattern,
CAKE Book maintains wiki-style pages with bidirectional links, source
metadata, hardware and CANN-version tags, trust and recency weights, and
an error notebook for recurring Ascend/CANN development failures. Human
review remains available for proposed knowledge and repository updates.
The design enables knowledge reuse in later CAKE runs; its causal effect
on success and performance is not isolated by the current evaluation
(Section [6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Operational Evidence for CAKE Book ‣ 6 Evidence from CANN-Bench and Operator Campaigns ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")).

CAKE Book complements the static references packaged with individual
skills. Static skill references capture stable procedures such as
artifact schemas, prompt contracts, code templates, and evaluation
commands. CAKE Book captures knowledge that changes with experience:
version-specific compiler behavior, newly observed CANN packaging traps,
operator-family tiling lessons, 950 Regbase/SIMT notes, profiler
interpretations, and workarounds that have only recently been validated.
When a skill needs such context, it can query CAKE Book as a task-time
reference source. The returned context is ranked not only by semantic
similarity, but also by link structure, evidence quality, hardware and
software compatibility, freshness, and human review status.

CAKE Book supports both retrieval and updates. For retrieval, an agent
or skill submits the current task context, retrieves relevant wiki pages
and linked error notes, ranks them by evidence, and packs the result
into an agent-ready reference. For updates, a completed run contributes
new observations: a compiler error and its fix, a profiler bottleneck
and the code change that removed it, a DSL route that repeatedly failed
for an operator family, or a human review note that corrects an agent
assumption. CAKE Book deduplicates these observations, attaches
provenance, and exposes them for review before they become trusted
references for future agents.

### 5.2 Run Evidence from the CAKE CI Platform

The Self-Evolving Agent observes CAKE through the CAKE CI Platform. The
platform standardizes generation and evolution runs and exposes a CLI
through which an agent can inspect run status, logs, and artifacts. For
each run, the agent can retrieve the operator contract, generated
PyTorch reference, functional form, DSL baseline, AscendC project files,
build logs, CANN package and install logs, evaluate.py outputs,
profiling CSVs, skill traces, PROGRESS.md, evolution reports, Advisor
state, issue or pull-request links, and user annotations. These
artifacts preserve both successful paths and failed attempts, which is
essential because many reusable CAKE lessons are negative: which route
compiled but failed precision, which template broke on non-aligned
shapes, or which Advisor suggestion did not transfer to a neighboring
operator family.

The CI interface also makes self-evolution measurable. Runs can be
grouped by operator family, DSL route, target chip, CANN version, input
mode, evaluation case type, and final status. This lets CAKE Book
distinguish local anecdotes from repeated patterns and lets the
Self-Evolving Agent detect regressions after router, template, Advisor,
or reference changes. Linking an update to its source runs also allows
later evaluations to check whether the same failure recurs.

### 5.3 Self-Evolving Agent

The Self-Evolving Agent runs continuously, checking newly available CAKE
CI Platform runs. It reads the corresponding artifacts, and records
observations through CAKE Book. Its daily work resembles an engineer’s
maintenance loop: summarize recent CI successes and failures, identify
repeated failure modes, compare them with existing CAKE Book pages,
notice when a previously useful rule becomes stale, and identify cases
where a dynamic lesson should become part of the repository.

When the observation is purely knowledge-oriented, the Self-Evolving
Agent interacts with CAKE Book directly. For example, it can add a new
error-note page for a CANN compiler diagnostic, link it to the affected
operator family and CANN version, attach the run IDs that demonstrate
the workaround, and mark the page as pending human review. When the
observation implies a code or repository change, the agent opens an
issue or pull request against the CAKE repository. Typical pull requests
include adding a static skill reference, improving a DSL prompt,
tightening a lowering check, documenting a new Advisor rule, extending
an evaluation audit, or updating router guidance for a hardware-specific
path. Merging remains a human decision; the agent proposes changes and
attaches evidence, while maintainers decide whether the evidence is
sufficient.

This separation keeps the self-evolving loop auditable. CAKE Book can
absorb fresh, uncertain, or version-specific experience quickly without
silently rewriting the public pipeline. Repository changes are slower
and require review, but once merged they improve the baseline behavior
of all later agents. In this sense, CAKE Book is the fast memory of the
system, while the static skill references, router rules, templates, and
Advisor rules are the stabilized memory.

### 5.4 Reference Promotion and Governance

Reference promotion is the bridge between dynamic and static knowledge.
A CAKE Book entry becomes a candidate for promotion when it is
repeatedly useful, supported by concrete run evidence, scoped to clear
hardware and software versions, and stable enough that future agents
should see it without issuing a live CAKE Book query. The Self-Evolving
Agent prepares the promotion by linking successful and failing runs,
summarizing the lesson, identifying the affected skill or rule file, and
opening an issue or pull request. Human reviewers then check whether the
proposed reference is correct, sufficiently general, and safe to apply
across future runs.

Governance is especially important because Ascend/CANN behavior changes
across hardware and software versions. CAKE Book entries therefore carry
provenance: run IDs, operator families, target chip, CANN and torch-npu
versions, input shapes, pass/fail status, profiler files, and reviewer
notes. Conflicting evidence does not overwrite older knowledge; it
creates versioned or scoped pages. Stale-rule detection is handled in
the same evidence-backed way: when CI runs show that a promoted rule no
longer helps or begins to harm a route, the Self-Evolving Agent records
the contradiction in CAKE Book and opens a follow-up issue or pull
request for human review.

Together, these components support knowledge reuse across runs. CAKE
agents retrieve current lessons from CAKE Book during generation, CAKE
CI Platform captures the full evidence trail of their attempts, the
Self-Evolving Agent monitors that trail around the clock, and stable
lessons move back into static skill references through reviewed pull
requests. Operator-level optimization supplies the observations;
repository review determines which lessons become part of the shared
generation workflow.

## 6 Evidence from CANN-Bench and Operator Campaigns

#### Setup.

The evaluation target is the official CANN-Bench v1.1 task set on Ascend
950PR, comprising 53 operators across difficulty levels 1–4, with 20
standard and 80 hidden cases per operator. We use the October 15, 2026
leaderboard snapshot, which selects the best result for each operator
separately in each case set across benchmark revisions 1.1.0–1.1.2. The
per-operator *benchsite score* is out of 100, with compile,
functional-correctness, and performance weights of $`0.2`$, $`0.3`$, and
$`0.5`$ under cann-bench-eq4-v1.

#### Operator completion.

All 53 operators compile in both case sets. CAKE passes all 1,060
standard cases ($`100\%`$) and 4,167 of 4,240 hidden cases
($`98.28\%`$). All 53 operators pass every standard case, and 38 pass
every hidden case.

#### Correctness and performance.

The benchmark score includes performance as well as correctness. CAKE
achieves mean operator scores of 79.31 on the standard set and 77.95 on
the hidden set. The overall mean is 78.63 out of 100, averaging equally
over the 53 operators and the two case sets. Correctness is the property
that CAKE’s acceptance criteria enforce; the remaining score reflects
opportunities for further correctness and performance improvement.

[7](#S6.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Correctness and performance. ‣ 6 Evidence from CANN-Bench and Operator Campaigns ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")

Figure 7: CAKE’s aggregated results by difficulty level on Ascend 950PR.
Levels 1–4 contain 8, 16, 21, and 8 operators. Left: mean operator
score, with a maximum of 100. Right: case pass rate, computed over 20

#### Score profiles across difficulty.

Figure [7](#S6.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Correctness and performance. ‣ 6 Evidence from CANN-Bench and Operator Campaigns ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
separates the results by difficulty. Standard-set case pass rate is
$`100\%`$ at every level, while mean scores are 86.86, 82.07, 76.32, and
74.11 for levels 1–4. On the hidden set, case pass rates are $`100\%`$,
$`99.22\%`$, $`98.21\%`$, and $`94.84\%`$, with mean scores of 91.76,
80.31, 76.46, and 63.34. Thus, functional coverage remains high across
levels, while the lower scores on the harder tasks identify
opportunities for further kernel optimization.

### 6.1 Router Observations

The evaluation ledger illustrates why routing uses operator features as
well as historical scores. In the current ledger, DSL-A’s raw mean
exceeds DSL-C’s by $`0.105`$, while the difficulty-adjusted scalar
abilities reported in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Adaptive Routing and Generation ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
are statistically indistinguishable. The per-dimension model then
restores operator dependence: the four worked decisions in
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ The routing loop. ‣ 3 Adaptive Routing and Generation ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
select three different tracks, with data movement, blocking, and
scheduling/reduction features changing the ordering.

The decision records contain the operator features, feasible tracks,
ability estimates, and skill versions needed to reconstruct each choice.
The examples show how CAKE adapts track selection to the requested
operator, rather than always choosing the track with the highest raw
mean score.

### 6.2 Operational Evidence for CAKE Book

CAKE CI records the artifacts from which a knowledge entry is created,
CAKE Book preserves its provenance and review state, and skills can
retrieve the result as task-time context. On the write side of this
loop, the diagnostics a campaign produces while debugging one operator
are retained in the shared layer instead of remaining in the case
directory, so a later run on an unrelated operator can retrieve them.

The evaluated CAKE workflow uses CAKE Book together with static
references and the Router. The records complement those end-to-end
results by showing how knowledge is captured, reviewed, and made
available to subsequent tasks.

## 7 Scope and Future Directions

The CANN-Bench results cover 53 operators on both standard and hidden
case sets. Router decision records illustrate operator-aware track
selection, the EngramGateFusion campaign demonstrates iterative kernel
optimization, and the CAKE Book records describe cross-task knowledge
reuse. The aggregate benchmark results use Ascend 950PR; the Router
examples and EngramGateFusion campaign retain their Ascend 910B/910C
settings.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Ascend 950 Vector: Regbase SIMD and SIMT ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
documents the programming paths and generation logic for Ascend 950.

Further development will extend Evolution to additional operator
families and expand the reusable knowledge available through CAKE Book.
Future evaluations will examine routing and retrieval configurations
under matched task sets and run budgets, and follow knowledge from CI
diagnostics through reuse and reviewed reference updates. The aim is to
improve operator coverage and performance while keeping generation cost
and expert review effort practical.

## 8 Conclusion

CAKE organizes Ascend operator engineering around a unit larger than a
generated kernel snippet: a deployable custom operator accompanied by
its contract, reference, lowering artifacts, package, binding,
evaluation record, and profile. Adaptive routing selects among changing
code-generation tracks from accumulated operator evidence; Evolution
mode searches within one operator contract using on-device feedback; and
CAKE Book with the Self-Evolving Agent carries lessons across runs under
human review.

The aggregated CANN-Bench results show full standard-set case coverage
and $`98.28\%`$ hidden-set case coverage across 53 operators on Ascend
950PR. The EngramGateFusion case study shows that Evolution mode can
improve an already-correct operator under on-device feedback.

## Appendix A Ascend 950 Vector: Regbase SIMD and SIMT

This appendix documents how CAKE generates and adapts operator code for
the Ascend 950 series. The 950 (a5, chip C310, device_type=950,
\_\_DAV_C310\_\_) shares its *Cube* primitive set with the earlier
a2/910B (C220); the divergence is on the *vector* side. Two 950-only
paths live on that side: *Regbase*, a register-level SIMD path for
latency-sensitive kernels with regular access patterns, and SIMT, a
multi-thread execution model for operators whose memory access or
control flow is data-dependent.
Sections [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Register-level operand model ‣ Appendix A Ascend 950 Vector: Regbase SIMD and SIMT ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
and [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 SIMT block resources ‣ Appendix A Ascend 950 Vector: Regbase SIMD and SIMT ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
describe the hardware resources.
Section [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Path selection ‣ Appendix A Ascend 950 Vector: Regbase SIMD and SIMT ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
gives the path-selection logic;
Sections [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Regbase code generation ‣ Appendix A Ascend 950 Vector: Regbase SIMD and SIMT ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
and [A.5](#A1.SS5 "A.5 SIMT code generation ‣ Appendix A Ascend 950 Vector: Regbase SIMD and SIMT ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
describe generated kernels, validation signals, and the SIMT
programming-model catalogue.

### A.1 Register-level operand model

Where the 910 path issues whole-tensor operations over UB-resident
LocalTensors (*membase*), the 950 exposes a register-level *MicroAPI*
programmed through @vf micro-functions. The hardware-specific
code-generation choices are therefore:

- •
  Register batches: RegTensor\<T\> holds a fixed VREG_SIZE-byte vector
  register rather than an arbitrarily large UB buffer.
- •
  Predication, not counts: active lanes are carried by a MaskReg
  predicate passed to every op, replacing the membase count argument.
- •
  Explicit addressing: gather/scatter index by raw byte offset with no
  bounds check. The regbase path offers LoadUnAlign/StoreUnAlign for
  UB$`\leftrightarrow`$register movement, enabling *unaligned* access.
- •
  MicroAPI: add/sub/exp/log exist on both paths but operate on registers
  in the 950 MicroAPI. Operations without a supported register-level
  lowering, such as widening Mull or reading back a Squeeze count,
  retain their membase implementation.

|            |                          |                              |
|------------|--------------------------|------------------------------|
|            | Membase                  | Regbase                      |
| Residency  | LocalTensor in UB        | RegTensor in VREG            |
| API        | whole-tensor AscendC::\* | AscendC::Reg::\* / MicroAPI  |
| Addressing | block-strided aligned    | can be unaligned             |
| Masking    | count argument           | explicit MaskReg predicate   |
| Movement   | DataCopy (TPipe queue)   | Load(Un)Align/Store(Un)Align |

Table 5: Membase and Regbase operand models: data residency, addressing,
masking, and transfer operations.

#### How Regbase reshapes the compute ceiling.

Regbase is an architectural shift from classical SIMD to a *dual-issue,
register-based SIMD* design: @vf kernels run micro-instructions directly
on RegTensor operands held in the vector register file. Whereas each
membase vector operation reads from UB and writes back, Regbase keeps
the working set resident in registers across the micro-kernel. Removing
those UB round trips moves the throughput limit from UB bandwidth toward
instruction issue, widened by dual issue.

### A.2 SIMT block resources

Each AI Vector core exposes a SIMT block that runs up to 2 048 threads
organized in 32-thread warps, with warp-level shuffle, vote, and
reduction intrinsics and 11-operation atomics on both on-chip and global
memory. SIMT threads access the *DataCache* partition of the Unified
Buffer—at most 128 KB, with the remaining UB capacity reserved for the
SIMD path—and synchronize through block-wide barriers.

### A.3 Path selection

The capability gate of
Section [3](#S3 "3 Adaptive Routing and Generation ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
first determines whether a supported execution track exists. On the 950,
data-dependent, non-contiguous access selects SIMT; otherwise,
register-level DSL coverage and the known gap list select Regbase or the
membase fallback.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 8: Target and path routing. check_device.sh reports the chip
generation, which admits the 910 lane or the two 950-specific lanes. On
the 950, operators with data-dependent non-contiguous access take SIMT;
the remainder use Regbase when the register-level DSL covers the kernel
and fall back to membase when it does not. The SIMT model-selection
questions Q1–Q6 are given in
Appendix [A.5](#A1.SS5 "A.5 SIMT code generation ‣ Appendix A Ascend 950 Vector: Regbase SIMD and SIMT ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU").

### A.4 Regbase code generation

The Regbase generation path uses explicit register operations to reduce
UB transfers or improve addressing and instruction scheduling.
Table [5](#A1.T5 "Table 5 ‣ A.1 Register-level operand model ‣ Appendix A Ascend 950 Vector: Regbase SIMD and SIMT ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
contrasts its operand model with membase. CAKE uses the DSL-C lowering
skills to generate this code.

#### When the router selects Regbase.

Three signal classes trigger the path: (1) regbase-only
micro-instructions — kernels using DataCopyGather, Histograms, and other
950 register-based micro-instructions that have no equivalent in the
AscendC API; (2) unaligned UB access — kernels that require non-aligned
access into the Unified Buffer; (3) low-latency kernels — small blocks
that fit a single register and high-iteration inner loops. Membase
remains the default; Regbase is attempted only when DSL-C supports all
required operations.

#### Generated code artifacts.

The Regbase path emits a @vf vector-function kernel with the structure
in
Figure [9](#A1.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Generated code artifacts. ‣ A.4 Regbase code generation ‣ Appendix A Ascend 950 Vector: Regbase SIMD and SIMT ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU"):
register and mask allocation followed by CeilDiv(len, VREG_LANES) loop
iterations. The mask handles the final partial iteration. Reusable
templates cover lookup-table/gather, compaction/filtering, and
histogram/scatter operations. Post-processing places the generated code
in CAKE’s operator project and renames the entry point to match its
binding. Migration from an existing membase kernel proceeds one region
at a time, checking bit-exact agreement with the original implementation
after each conversion. Regions without a supported register-level
lowering remain in membase form.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 9: @vf Regbase kernel skeleton. In this pattern, narrow I/O
(bf16/int8) is widened to RegTensor\<float\> on load via LoadDist and
packed back on store; computation uses float registers.

#### Compiler and profiler checks.

CAKE checks whether the conversion reduces memory traffic and execution
time using the following signals:

- •
  PipeBarrier removal — same-pipe (V$`\to`$V) barriers disappear,
  freeing instruction/pipeline slots; barriers remain only across pipes
  (MTE2$`\to`$V, V$`\to`$MTE3).
- •
  Lower load/store ratio — register residency removes UB round-trips
  that membase incurs.
- •
  Fewer wall cycles — cannsim reports Regbase $`<`$ membase on the same
  case, with a per-pipe split identifying the dominant pipe.

These are read from cannsim record ./test_aclnnop -s Ascend950
--gen-report and, for per-instruction attribution, msprof op simulator
(per-instruction CSV mapped back to source lines).

#### Validation without 950 hardware.

In the absence of 950 hardware, CAKE offers a simulator-only path backed
by cannsim or msprof that enables preliminary validation.

### A.5 SIMT code generation

Membase and Regbase execute predicated vector instructions over
UB-resident or register-resident data. Some operators, including gather,
histogram, and top-k selection, involve data-dependent addresses or
control flow. Such patterns are not inherently inexpressible in SIMD:
supported gather/scatter operations, masking, and staged data movement
can implement many of them. However, some irregular patterns require
additional transfers, predication, or serial processing, depending on
the available APIs and lowering support. SIMT provides an alternative
implementation path for these cases.

The 950 SIMT execution model can reduce these overheads using the block
resources summarized in
Section [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 SIMT block resources ‣ Appendix A Ascend 950 Vector: Regbase SIMD and SIMT ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU").
The capability gate of
Section [3](#S3 "3 Adaptive Routing and Generation ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU")
determines whether an operator can enter the SIMT track at all. The path
is taken when two additional conditions hold beyond the Regbase/membase
split: (i) the operator exhibits irregular or data-dependent memory
access, and (ii) the irregular access is *non-contiguous*—contiguous
scans with data-dependent predicates can remain on the SIMD path when
supported by the available operations. Once on the SIMT path, a
six-question decision tree
(Figure [10](#A1.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ A.5 SIMT code generation ‣ Appendix A Ascend 950 Vector: Regbase SIMD and SIMT ‣ CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU"))
refines the choice among three programming models that trade generality
for co-processor use. The simt-codegen skill implements this selection
and generates the corresponding kernel structure.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 10: SIMT model selection. Questions Q1–Q2 gate entry to the SIMT
path; Q3–Q6 choose among three programming models. Model A is a
CUDA-like \_\_global\_\_ kernel; Model B bridges SIMT threads into the
AscendC entry via asc_vf_call; Model C adds a \_\_simd_vf\_\_ stage that
offloads vectorizable arithmetic to the SIMD pipe after SIMT has
performed the irregular access.

#### Three programming models.

Model A (*pure SIMT*) is the most general: a single \_\_global\_\_
kernel launched with four-argument \<\<\<blocks, threads, ubuf,
stream\>\>\> syntax, compiled with the -cce-enable-puresimt flag. It
supports templates, struct arguments, and the full SIMT intrinsic set
(warp shuffle, vote, atomics, cache hints) but cannot call the AscendC
Micro API (LoadAlign, DataCopy, etc.). This model suits operators whose
compute is entirely irregular—histograms, hash-table insertion, stream
compaction—and whose output can be written directly to global memory.

Model B (*SIMT VF bridge*) wraps the per-thread compute in a
\_\_simt_vf\_\_ free function dispatched from an \_\_aicore\_\_ entry
via asc_vf_call. The three-argument launch integrates with msopgen
project scaffolding (tiling macros, REGISTER_TILING_DEFAULT), making it
the default for operators that fit the standard CANN host/device
contract—gather, cumulative sum, top-$`k`$ with warp reductions.

Model C (*hybrid SIMT+SIMD*) extends Model B for operators that fuse an
irregular access phase with a regular vectorizable phase. A
\_\_simt_vf\_\_ function performs the data-dependent read and stages
results into the DataCache; a \_\_simd_vf\_\_ function then runs the
same SIMD vector pipe used by the Regbase path (adds, relu, exp) over
the staged data; finally, DataCopy moves the result to global memory.
The benefit of offloading arithmetic to SIMD depends on the workload and
must be evaluated together with data-staging and synchronization costs;
low SIMD utilization alone does not establish negligible overhead. A
variant of Model C handles fused reductions (softmax, layer
normalization): since \_\_simd_vf\_\_ cannot compile cross-element
reductions (ReduceMax, ReduceSum), these are placed in the
\_\_aicore\_\_ entry function using high-level AscendC APIs.
````
